title: Raise a ratcheting jack stand's saddle three notches and push its locking handle down to check it
instruction: Raise the jack stand's saddle three notches from its lowest position, let it settle on the ratchet, then push the locking handle down to check that it is locked, then let go.
context: Before an oil change or a tire rotation at home, people set each jack stand to the height they need by pulling its ratchet bar up a few notches. The maker's manual says: "Adjust height by pulling up on ratchet bar. The weight of the locking handle should secure the ratchet bar in desired position. To confirm this, simply push down on the locking handle." A pawl that only partly engages is the known failure: in a 2020 recall of other 3-ton stands (NHTSA 20E-016), "the jack stand pawl may disengage from the extension lifting post, allowing the stand to drop suddenly". The robot must count the notches, set the bar down on the pawl and check the lock.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the arm bases, x forward, y to the robot's left, heights above the bench (the table) top. One Big Red T43002 3-ton steel jack stand (one of its pair; published lifting range 11-1/4 to 16-3/4 in) stands upright on the bench, its ratchet bar's axis at (40.0, -6.0), its locking handle hanging at the front, toward the robot, its saddle's groove running front to back. Its ratchet bar is at its lowest position (the saddle's top 28.6 cm above the bench) and the handle is down, its pawl home in the bar's teeth. Sizes estimated from maker photos: a four-leg stamped-steel frame 23 cm square at the feet and 24 cm tall, topped by a square column head; a 26 mm square ratchet bar with teeth 5 mm deep on its front face, eleven positions spaced evenly over the published range (13.97 mm apart), so three notches up puts the saddle's top at 32.8 cm (12.9 in); a U saddle 70 x 56 mm over its ears; a 10 mm bent-rod locking handle, its grip sleeve 10 cm in front of and 5 cm below its pin (the pin placed for the simulation). Masses from the parts' sizes and steel's density: bar and saddle 1.62 kg, frame 1.42 kg, handle with pawl 0.25 kg (3.3 kg in all). Arms start at the ready pose, grippers open.
scoring: 1.0: the bar locked three notches up (resting on the pawl at the third notch, its slide reading at most 1.5 mm from that notch, and the pawl fully home: the locking handle's hinge at most 1.4 degrees above its down stop, at least 3 mm of the pawl's 4.5 mm still under the tooth), the handle's grip pushed down on top by a hand (contact on the grip's upper half for at least 0.25 s; in simulation an arm link within 0.6 mm of it for 5 control steps in a row) while the bar sat locked there and no hand held the bar (a bar lifted off and set back, or a handle lifted, needs a new check), then every arm link at least 5 mm from the bar, saddle, handle and column head, and the bar, handle and stand still (under 1 cm/s) for 1 s. 0.5: locked at the third notch and let go, but the handle never pushed down while it was (or not still for 1 s). 0.25: locked at any other notch (1, 2 or 4 to 10) and let go. 0: anything else, including doing nothing (the bar starts at its lowest position), the bar held up by a hand or left between notches, the pawl not fully home, a hand still on the bar, saddle, handle or column head at the end, and the stand tipped more than 5 degrees from upright at any moment (latched: a stand rocked that far under a car is unsafe). Not judged: where the stand ends up on the bench, hands on the frame's legs, and a hand on the column head before the end (off it by the end). In simulation the notch is read from the bar's slide joint and the pawl from the handle's hinge. Real trial: notches counted by clicks on the video and the saddle's height measured (32.8 cm at notch 3); the handle hangs at its stop; tipping (a foot lifting about 2 cm) and the push on the handle from the video; the push counts only if the hand stays on top for at least 0.25 s, no hand is on the bar or saddle at that moment and the bar is not lifted afterwards. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0.
reset_notes: Lift the locking handle, guide the bar down to its lowest position, let the handle drop, and stand the stand on its tape marks with the handle toward the robot. Under 30 seconds. In simulation the reset is exact.
fidelity: Real-size rigid bodies. Teeth (20 degree undercut) and pawl are convex hulls in contact; only the pawl under a tooth holds the bar, at every notch and at the bottom; the handle's weight swings it home. Changed for the sim: tooth tops 58 degrees, pin high and close to the teeth (pawl cams out at about 5 N). Simplified: slide joint for the bar; bar travel ends and handle stops are joint limits; the pawl passes the column wall (a slot in the real one); leg cut-outs count in mass only.
